# Executive Summary

# Data and Exploratory Data Analysis {#initial-analysis}

We have extended the 15-minute discharge data for the River Don at Parkhill from ten [water years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_year) in Part 1 to twenty-five for Part 2. We retain the 65 $m^3/s$ threshold and the Robson and Reed [@robson1999] independence criteria, which identifies `r nrow(peaks)` independent extreme flow events, an average of `r sprintf("%.2f", nrow(peaks) / n_years)` per year.

```{r tidyingthedata, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, tab.cap="Data used in this analysis, and the quality codes assigned to each reading"}
tidy_data_table
```

### Unchecked readings {#unchecked-readings}

We identified `r nrow(unchecked_model$unique_readings)` Unchecked readings falling within `r n_distinct(unchecked_model$in_windows$Event_ID)` of the standardised event windows (Table \@ref(tab:uncheckeddata)).

```{r uncheckeddata, results="asis", echo=FALSE}
if (!is.null(unchecked_model)) {
  knitr::kable(
    unchecked_model$table,
    format    = "markdown",
    align     = "llrrrrrr",
    col.names = c("Burst", "Event(s)", "Start", "Readings", "Duration (min)",
                  "Max flow (m³/s)", "RMSE (m³/s)", "Max abs. diff (m³/s)"),
    caption   = "Unchecked readings (code 254) within the event windows, compared with linear interpolation between the neighbouring checked readings. Dashed 1:1 line represents perfect agreement."
  )
}
```

We compared the original Unchecked readings with interpolated values to decide whether retaining these Unchecked readings was reasonable (Figure \@ref(fig:uncheckedscatter))

```{r uncheckedscatter, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Unchecked readings against the linear interpolation between neighbouring checked readings."}
if (!is.null(unchecked_model)) unchecked_model$plot
```

All Unchecked readings lie close to this line with a `RMSE` of `r sprintf("%.3f", unchecked_model$rmse)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ against discharge values of up to `r sprintf("%.0f", unchecked_model$max_q)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$, so these discrepancies are relatively small.

Although this does not prove that the Unchecked readings are completely accurate, it provides some reassurance that retaining them is unlikely to significantly affect the hydrograph shapes, and avoids unnecessary modification to the data.

### Suspect readings {#suspect-readings}

SEPA flags `r format(n_suspect, big.mark = ",")` readings (`r sprintf("%.2f", pct_suspect)`% of the record) as Suspect (code 150), meaning that the flow lies beyond the acceptable extrapolation limit of the gauge's stage-discharge relationship. As in Part 1, these readings are excluded. The largest Suspect reading is `r sprintf("%.1f", max_suspect)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$, and `r n_suspect_above` exceed the `r u_final` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ threshold. However, a reading below the threshold can still affect the shape of an event.

```{r suspecttext, results="asis", echo=FALSE}
if (is.null(suspect_model)) {
  cat("Albeit, none of the Suspect readings fall inside any of the", nrow(events),
      "event windows, so excluding them does not affect any of the hydrographs we model.\n")
} else {
  cat(sprintf(
    "%d Suspect readings, in %d separate bursts, fall inside %d of the %d event windows (Table \\@ref(tab:suspectdata)). Figure \\@ref(fig:suspecthydro) shows where they lie within the hydrographs of the affected events, alongside the interpolated values the model uses in their place.\n",
    n_suspect_model_readings, n_suspect_model_bursts, n_suspect_model_events, nrow(events)))
}
```

```{r suspectdata, results="asis", echo=FALSE}
if (!is.null(suspect_model)) {

  )
}
```

```{r suspecthydro, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Hydrographs of the events containing Suspect readings. The line shows the readings used in the model, which is the linear interpolation across each gap; points show the excluded Suspect readings; the dotted line is the threshold."}
if (!is.null(suspect_model_plot)) suspect_model_plot
```

## Exploratory Analysis {#exploratory-analysis}

To investigate the variation in hydrograph shape, the `r nrow(peaks)` independent extreme flow events are aligned at their maximum discharge, with the peak assigned time zero.

```{r Hydrograph, echo=FALSE}
hydrograph_overlay_plot
```

We observe significant variation in maximum discharge, the sharpness of peaks, and the rising and falling limbs.

The mean hydrograph smooths over important differences between individual events. Consequently, representing every event using an average hydrograph scaled by peak discharge fails to capture the full variability in an event.

## Standardising the hydrographs {#standardising-the-hydrographs}

Our analysis reveals that extreme flow events differ in duration, peak discharge, and the relative timing of peaks. Since these differences obscure the variation in hydrograph shape, we standardise the extreme flow events:

- Events are defined between rising and falling limb troughs.

- Time is rescaled to the interval [0,1], with zero and one representing event start and end respectively.

- Relative peak position is calculated as $\frac{\text{peak time} - \text{event start}}{\text{event duration}}$.

- Rising and falling limbs are rescaled separately to align all hydrograph peaks so that peak timing doesn't dominate the analysis.

- Discharge is divided by maximum flow, standardising hydrograph peaks to have value of one.

- Hydrographs are reconstructed using linear interpolation between 64 equally spaced, common points on the standardised time scale.

- The resulting data are arranged into a matrix ($Y$), with one row per event and 64 columns for each time point.

The original peak discharge, event duration and relative peak position are retained separately, allowing for the transformation of standardised hydrographs to their original discharge and time scales for subsequent model validation.

# Methods for representing hydrograph shape

The output of flood inundation models fit emulators. Since every input increases the number of runs to fit it, and each run is slow, we aim to minimise the number of inputs. After standardisation (Section \@ref(#standardising-the-hydrographs)), each of the ($N =$ `r nrow(Y)`) extreme flow events are summarised to `r n_grid` time points $u_j$, their standardised discharge $y_i(u_j)$, peak discharge $Q_i^{\text{peak}}$, duration $W_i$, and relative peak position $\tau_i$.

Using all of these `r n_grid + 3` values as emulator inputs would be impractical. We therefore considered five methods for reducing the number of parameters needed to represent hydrograph shape. These methods are polynomial regression, principal component analysis (PCA), wavelets, B-splines and a gamma-type function.

Most methods approximate each standardised hydrograph by a weighted sum of $K$ basis functions,

\begin{equation}
y_i(u) \approx \sum_{k=1}^{K} \theta_{ik}\,\phi_k(u),
(\#eq:basis)
\end{equation}

where $\phi_k(u)$ are the basis functions and $\theta_{ik}$ are the shape parameters for event $i$. The methods differ mainly in how these functions are chosen. Peak discharge, duration and relative peak position are retained separately, giving ($K+3$) parameters for each event. The exceptions are PCA, which first subtracts the mean curve before applying \@ref(eq:basis), and the gamma-type curve from our further reading, which is a nonlinear function of its parameters.

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{x}_i = \left(Q_i^{\text{peak}},\; W_i,\; \tau_i,\; \boldsymbol{\theta}_i\right).
(\#eq:inputs)
\end{equation}

The emulator therefore only needs $3 + K$ inputs, where $K$ is significantly smaller than the previous `r n_grid`.

## SEPA's Approach {#method-SEPA}

SEPA's current approach is our baseline. It uses a fix-shape hydrograph, which is scaled according to maximum discharge. The baseline was constructed by averaging the standardised hydrographs (from \@ref(standardising-the-hydrographs)) without aligning their peaks, (as SEPA does not do so). The unaligned curves $\tilde{y}_i(u)$, are then averaged across extreme flow events,

\begin{equation}
\bar{y}(u) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{l=1}^{N} \tilde{y}_l(u),
(\#eq:sepa)
\end{equation}

and rescaled to have a peak value of one,

\begin{equation}
\hat{y}(u) = \frac{\bar{y}(u)}{\max_u \bar{y}(u)}.
(\#eq:sepa-2)
\end{equation}

The fitted hydrograph for extreme flow event $i$ is obtained by stretching $\hat{y}$ to the extreme flow event's duration $W_i$ and multiplying it by its peak discharge $Q_i^{\text{peak}}$. This means every event shares the same shape and differs only in its height and length. To test how well this shape predicts an event it has not seen, each event is also compared with the average of the other $N - 1$ events only.

Unlike SEPA's current approach, our baseline allows duration ($W_i$) to vary between events. This means the observed hydrographs now obtained may be more accurate than the strictly fixed-duration approach.

## Evaluation criteria {#evaluation-criteria}

We compared the methods using three criteria: accuracy, parsimony, and fitness for purpose [@wilson2026lec5]. These helped choose the initial number of parameters for each method (Sections @ref(#method-polynomial) - @ref(#method-other)) and the final comparison in (Section @ref(Comparison)).

**Accuracy:** We measured how closely each method reconstructed the observed hydrographs using the root mean squared error (RMSE): 

\begin{equation}
\text{RMSE}_i = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{`r n_grid`}\textstyle\sum_{j}\big(\hat{Q}_i(t_j) - Q_i(t_j)\big)^2}.
(\#eq:rmse)
\end{equation}

As flood inundation use actual discharge values not standardised values, we calculated errors after converting the reconstructed hydrographs back to their original discharge and time scales.

For methods that estimate a shared shape or basis across extreme flow events (SEPA's approach, PCA and the wavelet coefficient selection), we used leave-one-out cross-validation. Each event was excluded in turn, while the shared model was refitted using the remaining $N - 1$ events The events excluded were then reconstructed using this fitted model.

For methods where each event was fitted separately (polynomial, B-spline and gamma-type), leaving out an event does not change the other fitted curves. So, we randomly divided the events into `r length(train_floods)` training and `r length(test_floods)` test events to compare the reconstruction errors and guide our selection of parameters.  

**Parsimony:** As the shape parameters are inputs to the emulator, a method is required to ensure fewer parameters is preferable, provided that they still reconstruct the hydrographs accurately. Strong correlations between parameters may also complicate modelling their uncertainty. Thus, we compared both the number of shape parameters and their correlations across events.

**Fitness for purpose:** The `RMSE` measures overall reconstruction accuracy, but it doesn't determine whether the method represents a valid range of hydrograph shapes. So, we also measure errors in peak discharge, peak timing and total flow volume [@wilson2026lec5]:

\begin{align}
\text{Peak error}_i &= \max_j \hat{Q}_i(t_j) - \max_j Q_i(t_j), (\#eq:peak)\\
\text{Timing error}_i &= \hat{t}_{i}^{\,\text{peak}} - t_{i}^{\,\text{peak}}, (\#eq:timing)\\
\text{Volume error}_i &= 100 \times \frac{\int \hat{Q}_i(t)\,dt - \int Q_i(t)\,dt}{\int Q_i(t)\,dt}\ \%, (\#eq:volume)
\end{align}

Flow volumes were calculated using the trapezium rule. As all methods except SEPA's baseline align peaks to their observed positions, timing errors are expected to be small by construction. This measure is therefore most useful for assessing the baseline.

Finally, a method must be able to represent the variation seen in extreme flow events, not just reproduce typical hydrographs. This is assesed further in Section @ref(uncertainty), where uncertainty in the shape parameters is modelled.

## Polynomial regression {#method-polynomial}
The first method uses polynomial regression of a degree-p polynomial in time to approximate each standardised hydrograph:
\begin{equation}
y_i(u_j) \approx \theta_{i0} + \theta_{i1}u_j + \theta_{i2}u_j^2 + \dots + \theta_{ip}u_j^p, \qquad j = 1, \dots, `r n_grid`.
(\#eq:poly)
\end{equation}

For each event, the $p+1$ coefficients were estimated by ordinary least squares,
\begin{equation}
\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_i = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y}_i
(\#eq:OLS)
\end{equation}

where $X$ is the `r n_grid`$\times(p+1)$ design matrix with columns $1,u,\ldots,u^p$, and $\mathbf{y}_i$ contains the `r n_grid` standardised discharge values. These coefficients form the shape parameters of each event.

To choose the degree $p$, we tested degrees 2–15, comparing errors across training and test events (Figure \@ref(fig:polychoice)). We also examined the significance of the highest-order coefficient (Table \@ref(tab:polysig)). However,  these tests are less reliable as neighbouring discharge readings are correlated, violating the independence assumption used to calculate standard errors.

```{r polysig, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%"}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(degree = degrees, prop = sprintf("%.2f", prop_significant)),
  format    = "markdown",
  col.names = c("Degree $p$", "Proportion of events with $\\theta_p$ significant at 5%"),
  align     = "cc",
  caption   = "Proportion of events for which the highest-order polynomial term is significant at the 5% level."
)
```

Figure \@ref(fig:polychoice) shows that the errors generally decrease with increasing degree, particularly when moving to higher odd degrees. Degree 7 gives a substantial improvement over degree 6 in RMSE, peak and timing errors, while higher degrees offer smaller improvements relative to the additional parameters. We therefore selected $p =$ `r p_chosen`, representing each hydrograph using eight shape parameters.

```{r polychoice, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Average absolute errors for training and test events by polynomial degree.", out.width="80%", fig.align='center'}
plot_choice(poly_choice, "Polynomial degree")
```


## Principal component analysis (PCA) {#method-pca}

Unlike the polynomial, PCA estimates its basis functions from the hydrographs themselves, finding the curves that best describe the pattern of variation between events [@wilson2026lec4]. 

We arranged the standardised hydrographs into a  `r nrow(Y)` $\times$ `r n_grid` matrix $Y$, with one row per event, and centred each column by subtracting the mean curve $\bar{y}(u_j)$. No further scaling was needed, as all discharge values were already standardised. The principle components $\phi_1, \phi_2, \dots$, are the eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix, ordered by the amount of variation they explain. Each hydrograph is then approximated by

\begin{equation}
y_i(u_j) \approx \bar{y}(u_j) + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \xi_{ik}\,\phi_k(u_j), \qquad \xi_{ik} = \sum_{j=1}^{`r n_grid`} \big(y_i(u_j) - \bar{y}(u_j)\big)\,\phi_k(u_j),
(\#eq:pca)
\end{equation}

The scores $\xi_{i1}, \dots, \xi_{iK}$ are the shape parameters for event $i$. Unlike polynomial coefficients, PCA scores are uncorrelated across the fitted events by construction, making their uncertanity easier to model.

```{r pcaloadings, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.cap="The first three principal components against standardised time.", out.width="80%", fig.align='center'}
matplot(grid_u, pca_result$rotation[, 1:3], type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2,
        col = c("#AA1945", "#5298BC", "#174B67"),
        xlab = "Standardised time u", ylab = "Loading", main = "")
abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
legend("bottomright", c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3"), lty = 1, lwd = 2,
       col = c("#AA1945", "#5298BC", "#174B67"), bty = "n")
```

Figure \@ref(fig:pcaloadings) shows that the first three principal components explain `r round(100 * cum_var[3])`% of the variation. PC1 (`r round(100 * cum_var[1])`%) mainly describes event width, PC2 contrasts the rising and falling limbs, and PC3 captures the difference in the steepness of the rising limb. All three are close to zero at the aligned peak, where the standardised hydrographs have almost no variation. 

We select $K$ using cumulative variance explained (Figure \@ref(fig:pcacumvar)) and reconstruction errors (Figure \@ref(fig:pcachoice)). For the leave-one-our check, the mean curve and components were recalculated without each excluded event before reconstructing it. Six components explained approximately 95% of the variation with little improvement in leave-one-out RMSE from adding a seventh. We therefore selected $K=6$, reducing each hydrograph to six shape parameters.


```{r pcacumvar, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4.5, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}

ggplot(
  data.frame(K = seq_along(cum_var), cum_var = cum_var),
  aes(x = K, y = cum_var)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "#AA1945") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 6, linetype = "dotted",
             colour = "#5298BC") +
  annotate("text", x = 35, y = 0.93,
           label = "95% variance explained",
           colour = "#AA1945", size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 7.3, y = 0.35,
           label = "K = 6 selected",
           colour = "#5298BC", hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Cumulative Variance Explained by PCA",
    x = "Number of components (K)",
    y = "Cumulative proportion of variation"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```
\begin{center}
\captionof{figure}{Cumulative proportion of variation explained by the first $K$ principal components, with the dashed line at 95\%.\label{fig:pcacumvar}}
\end{center}

```{r pcachoice, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Average absolute errors, in-sample and leave-one-out, by number of principal components", out.width="80%", fig.align='center'}
plot_choice(pca_choice, "Number of components K")
```

## Wavelets {#method-wavelets}
Wavelets represent a hydrograph using functions localised in time and scale, making them useful for capturing sharp peaks and smaller fluctuations without changing the whole fitted curve [@wilson2026lec4]. We applied the discrete wavelet transformation (DWT) to each standardised hydrograph, separating it into a smooth component and details at three resolution levels:

\begin{equation}
y_i(u) = \sum_{k} a_{ik}\,\varphi_k(u) + \sum_{j=1}^{`r wav_levels`}\sum_{k} d_{ijk}\,\psi_{jk}(u),
(\#eq:wavelet)
\end{equation}

where $a_{ik}$ are the smooth coefficients and $d_{ijk}$ are the detail coefficients at scale $j$ and location $k$. At `r wav_levels` levels, each `r n_grid`-point hydrograph gives `r n_grid / 2^wav_levels` smooth and `r n_grid - n_grid / 2^wav_levels` detail coefficients, allowing exact reconstruction if all are retained. 

To reduce the number of parameters, we kept all `r n_grid / 2^wav_levels` smooth coefficients and selected the $M$ detail coefficient positions with the largest average absolute values across events. The same positions were retained for every event, so each parameter represents the same feature.

We selected $M$ by comparing in-sample and leave-one-out reconstruction errors (Figure \@ref(fig:wavdecomp)). Peak error fell sharply up to $M = 5$, with little improvement thereafter, while `RMSE` decreased more gradually. We therefore retained five detail coefficients, giving 13 shape parameters. 

```{r wavdecomp, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Wavelet decomposition of event 1: the detail coefficients at each level and the smooth coefficients.", out.width="80%", fig.align='center'}
par(mfrow = c(4, 1), mar = c(2, 4, 2, 1))
plot(wt_example@W[[1]], type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "#5298BC", xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Level 1 detail (finest)")
plot(wt_example@W[[2]], type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "#5298BC", xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Level 2 detail")
plot(wt_example@W[[3]], type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "#5298BC", xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Level 3 detail (coarsest)")
plot(wt_example@V[[3]], type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "#174B67", xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Level 3 smooth")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)
```

```{r wavchoice, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Average absolute errors, in-sample and leave-one-out, by number of detail coefficients kept.", out.width="80%", fig.align='center'}
plot_choice(wav_choice, "Detail coefficients kept")
```

We also compared `haar`, `d4` and `la8` wavelets at different decomposition levels table \@ref(tab:wavsens). Increasing the number of levels did reduce the parameter count but generally also increased errors. At three levels, `la8` gave the lowest `RMSE`, ($3.34 \text{m}^3/\text{s}$), peak error ($0.98 \text{m}^3/\text{s}$) and volume error ($0.10\%$). So we selected `la8` with three levels and five detail coefficients.

```{r wavsens, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%"}
knitr::kable(
  wav_sensitivity, digits = 2, format = "markdown",
  col.names = c("Wavelet", "Levels", "Shape parameters", "RMSE (m³/s)",
                "Peak error (m³/s)", "Timing error (h)", "Volume error (%)"),
  caption = "Average absolute errors for different wavelets and numbers of levels, keeping the same number of detail coefficients."
)
```

## Other methods {#method-other}

As well as the three suggested methods we also considered two further methods, each addressing a weakness found above.

### B-splines {#method-bspline}
Unlike a single polynomial, B-splimnes represent a curve using smoothly joined polynomial pieces, allowimg for local changes without affecting the entire hydrograph [@ramsay2005functional]. We fitted cubic B-splines with equally spaced knots to each standardised event:

\begin{equation}
y_i(u_j) \approx \theta_{i0} + \sum_{l=1}^{L} \theta_{il}\,B_l(u_j)
(\#eq:bspline)
\end{equation}

where $B_l(u_j)$ are the spline basis functions and $\theta_{il}$ are estimated by least squares. We chose $L =$ `r n_basis_chosen`, giving `r n_basis_chosen + 1` fitted coefficients, close to the `r p_chosen + 1` used in polynomial regression, allowing comparison at similar complexity.


### A known hydrograph function (Gamma-type function) {#method-gamma}

The lectures suggest that a known function which approximates hydrographs may give parameters that can be interpreted. Thus, we considered a gamma-type hydrograph based on Nash, [@nash1957instantaneous]. This provides three interpretable parameters describing baseflow relative to peak discharge, peak timing and peak sharpness.

We fitted the function, with an additional baseflow term, separately to each standardised hydrograph using nonlinear least squares. Unlike the other methods, its parameters enter the model nonlinearly. This provides a more parsimonious alternative, although its shape is restricted to a single peak.

# Validation and comparison of methods {#Comparison}

```{r cmp-text-helpers, include = FALSE}
# Look up one value from the paired comparisons (Table 7) for the text below
pr_val <- function(comparison, metric, col) {
  paired_results[[col]][paired_results$comparison == comparison &
                          paired_results$metric == paired_metrics[[metric]]]
}
vs_sepa <- c("PCA minus SEPA (average shape)", "Wavelets minus SEPA (average shape)")
```

We now validate and compare all six approaches at their chosen settings. Errors are in real units and held-out wherever a method learns from other events (Section \@ref(evaluation-criteria)), so the comparison is like-for-like.

## How each method fits individual events {#validation-contrast}

```{r all-methods-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 10, fig.cap = "Observed (black) and fitted curves from each method for six contrasting extreme flow events: those with the earliest and latest peaks, the shortest and longest durations, and the flattest and sharpest peaks."}
plot_all_methods()
```

```{r residuals-all, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6.5, fig.cap = "Residuals against rescaled time for each method (grey: individual extreme flow events; coloured: average), with the five averages compared in the final panel."}
plot_all_residuals()
```

The polynomial method fits a single peak that is too low and broad, so it misses sharp and multi-peak extreme flow events (Figure \@ref(fig:all-methods-plot)), and its higher-order terms make the fit drift at the ends. Its residuals (Figure \@ref(fig:residuals-all)) are positive at the peak and negative either side for most events. The B-spline method shares this peak problem but fits the recession closely, with residuals near zero after $u \approx 0.6$. The gamma-type method fits worst, as each curve has a single peak and the same baseflow at both ends.

PCA reproduces single-peak events almost exactly and multi-peak events closely, though it underestimates some smaller peaks; its residuals are small, and largest on the rising limb. Wavelets are similarly accurate but show unrealistic dips, as every event keeps the same detail coefficients, and deviations at the ends from the periodic boundary. Residuals are correlated over time, which is harmless as the fits serve as a basis, not for inference.

## Accuracy and event features {#cmp-accuracy}

```{r cmp-main, echo=FALSE}
kable(cmp_main_tbl, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrrrrrr",
      col.names = c("Method", "$K$", "Inputs", "In-sample", "Held-out", "Held-out (\\% of peak)",
                    "Peak (m$^3$/s)", "Timing (h)", "Volume (\\%)", "Neg.", "Max $|r|$"),
      caption = "Comparison of SEPA's approach and the five methods at their chosen settings. Errors are average absolute values over extreme flow events, in real units.") %>%
  add_header_above(c(" " = 3, "RMSE (m$^3$/s)" = 3, "Held-out errors" = 3,
                     "Parameter behaviour" = 2), escape = FALSE) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("scale_down", "hold_position"), font_size = 9) %>%
  footnote(general = paste0(
    "$K$: number of shape parameters; Inputs: emulator inputs ($K$ plus peak flow, duration and peak position; SEPA uses peak flow). ",
    "Held-out: leave-one-out for SEPA, PCA and wavelets. The polynomial, B-spline and gamma-type are fitted to each event on its own, so their held-out and in-sample errors are identical; ",
    "for wavelets, leaving one event out does not change which coefficients are kept, so the two also coincide. ",
    "Gamma-type: the ", length(gamma_ok), " of ", nrow(Y), " events whose fit converged. ",
    "Neg.: events whose held-out curve has negative flow. Max $|r|$: largest absolute correlation between shape parameters across events. Bold: best in column."),
    general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = FALSE)
```

```{r cmp-features, echo=FALSE}
kable(cmp_feat_tbl, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrrrrr",
      col.names = c("Method", "Peak (m$^3$/s)", "Volume (\\%)", "90th pct.", "Worst",
                    "Duration (h)", "Volume (Mm$^3$)", "Volume bias (Mm$^3$)",
                    "Rising", "Falling"),
      caption = paste0("Event-relevant features and worst-case performance (held-out). Bias is the signed mean error (positive = overestimate). ",
                       "Above threshold: time and volume of flow above $u = ", u_final,
                       "$ m$^3$/s. RMSE by limb: before and after the observed peak.")) %>%
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Bias" = 2, "RMSE across events (m$^3$/s)" = 2,
                     "Above threshold $u$" = 3, "RMSE by limb (m$^3$/s)" = 2), escape = FALSE) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("scale_down", "hold_position"), font_size = 9)
```

```{r cmp-distribution, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Held-out errors for every extreme flow event, by method (log scale). Boxes show the middle 50\\% of events; points are individual events with unusually large errors."}
per_event_long_plot
```

Every method beats SEPA's fixed shape (Table \@ref(tab:cmp-main)), and PCA and wavelets beat it by an order of magnitude: held-out RMSE falls from `r sprintf("%.1f", cmp_text$rmse_sepa)` (SEPA) to `r sprintf("%.2f", cmp_text$rmse_pca)` (PCA) and `r sprintf("%.2f", cmp_text$rmse_wav)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ (wavelets). SEPA matches the peak by construction, so its errors are in shape: its peak is on average `r sprintf("%.0f", cmp_text$timing_sepa)` hours out, and it overstates volume by `r sprintf("%.0f", cmp_text$volume_sepa)`\%, or `r sprintf("%.1f", cmp_text$excess_sepa)` $\text{Mm}^3$ above $u$ (Table \@ref(tab:cmp-features)), which would overstate the extent and duration of inundation. The polynomial and B-spline methods underestimate the peak, which drives the extent of inundation, by `r sprintf("%.1f", cmp_text$peak_poly)` and `r sprintf("%.1f", cmp_text$peak_bspline)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$, and give negative flow in `r S("Polynomial", "neg_events")` events each. Their flattened peaks, like the gamma-type's, also let the maximum drift by `r sprintf("%.1f", min(sapply(c("Gamma-type", "Polynomial", "B-spline"), S, col = "timing_out")))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(sapply(c("Gamma-type", "Polynomial", "B-spline"), S, col = "timing_out")))` hours.

Wavelets have the lowest errors on most metrics, but give negative flow in `r S("Wavelets", "neg_events")` events (PCA: `r S("PCA", "neg_events")`). Even PCA's worst event (`r sprintf("%.1f", S("PCA", "rmse_max"))` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$) beats SEPA's average (Figure \@ref(fig:cmp-distribution)). PCA's RMSE rises only from `r sprintf("%.2f", cmp_text$rmse_pca_in)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", cmp_text$rmse_pca)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ when events are held out, so its basis carries over to new events.

## Parsimony and parameter behaviour {#cmp-parsimony}

```{r cmp-tradeoff, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Accuracy against number of shape parameters for every setting tried in Section 3 (log scale; leave-one-out for PCA and wavelets, all events for the per-event methods). Circled points are the chosen settings; the dashed line is SEPA's approach (leave-one-out)."}
tradeoff_long_plot
```

Each shape parameter adds an emulator input, and with it more inundation-model runs. For a given $K$, PCA usually gives the lowest errors (Figure \@ref(fig:cmp-tradeoff)), except for volume error, where it is in line with the other methods. At equal $K =$ `r ncol(wav_params)`, PCA's held-out RMSE is `r sprintf("%.2f", cmp_text$pca_at_wav_K)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ against wavelets' `r sprintf("%.2f", cmp_text$rmse_wav)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$, so wavelets' lower error at their chosen settings comes from extra parameters, not a better basis.

Simulating new events needs the joint distribution of the shape parameters, with every correlation estimated from `r nrow(Y)` events. PCA scores are uncorrelated by construction and gamma-type parameters weakly correlated (up to `r sprintf("%.2f", S("Gamma-type", "max_cor"))`), whereas polynomial coefficients are near-collinear (up to `r sprintf("%.2f", S("Polynomial", "max_cor"))`), and B-spline and wavelet coefficients reach `r sprintf("%.2f", S("B-spline", "max_cor"))` and `r sprintf("%.2f", S("Wavelets", "max_cor"))`. PCA's basis must be re-estimated as new events are recorded, whereas the wavelet basis is fixed, but both are cheap to fit.

## Are the differences real? {#cmp-paired}

```{r cmp-paired, echo=FALSE}
kable(select(paired_tbl, -Comparison), format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE,
                      align = "lrrrr",
                      col.names = c("Metric", "Mean difference", "95\\% bootstrap CI",
                                    "Events where first is better (\\%)", "Wilcoxon $p$"),
                      caption = "Paired comparison of held-out absolute errors over the same extreme flow events, grouped by comparison. A negative difference means the first-named method has smaller errors.") %>%
  pack_rows(index = table(paired_tbl$Comparison)) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), font_size = 9)
```

Paired comparisons on the same events, independent by the Robson & Reed criteria, using a bootstrap confidence interval and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Table \@ref(tab:cmp-paired)), show the differences are real. PCA and wavelets beat SEPA on RMSE and volume error for `r sprintf("%.0f", min(sapply(vs_sepa, function(cm) c(pr_val(cm, "rmse", "first_better"), pr_val(cm, "volume_error", "first_better")))))`\% of events, with similar peak errors, and PCA beats the B-spline on peak error for `r sprintf("%.0f", pr_val("PCA minus B-spline", "peak_error", "first_better"))`\%. Wavelets beat PCA on RMSE for `r sprintf("%.0f", pr_val("Wavelets minus PCA", "rmse", "first_better"))`\% of events, but PCA has the smaller peak error for `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 - pr_val("Wavelets minus PCA", "peak_error", "first_better"))`\%. Their RMSE difference of `r sprintf("%.2f", abs(cmp_text$wav_minus_pca))` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ is small next to their gain of about `r sprintf("%.0f", cmp_text$rmse_sepa - cmp_text$rmse_pca)` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ over SEPA, so the choice between them should rest on parsimony and parameter behaviour.

## Methods carried forward {#cmp-synthesis}

```{r cmp-synthesis, echo=FALSE}
kable(synthesis, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Method", "Accuracy (held-out RMSE)", "Event features", "Unusual events",
                    "Shape parameters", "Parameter behaviour", "Physical validity",
                    "Interpretability"),
      caption = "Summary of the comparison against the three criteria. The two methods carried forward to the uncertainty analysis are in bold.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), font_size = 8) %>%
  column_spec(1, width = "1.6cm") %>%
  column_spec(2:8, width = "1.5cm") %>%     # 8 columns fit a 16cm text width
  row_spec(which(synthesis$Method %in% c("PCA", "Wavelets")), bold = TRUE)
```

Table \@ref(tab:cmp-synthesis) summarises the trade-offs. We eliminate SEPA's approach, whose fixed shape cannot capture timing or volume; the polynomial and B-spline methods, which erode the peak and give negative flows; and the gamma-type method, which, though the most parsimonious and interpretable, cannot represent multi-peak events or different start and end flows, and has `r sprintf("%.1f", S("Gamma-type", "rmse_out") / S("PCA", "rmse_out"))` times PCA's RMSE. We carry PCA and wavelets forward to Section \@ref(uncertainty), as they differ usefully: PCA has the fewest, uncorrelated parameters, and wavelets the lowest error with a fixed basis. The final choice rests on how realistically each simulates new events.

# Uncertainty analysis {#uncertainty}

For the PCA and wavelet decomposition methods that we are taking forward, we now model the uncertainty in their parameters between hydrographs. Importantly, this allows us to move beyond the extreme flow events we have observed and simulate new hydrographs, and it means the uncertainty in hydrograph shape at extreme flows can be propagated through an emulator of the flood inundation model.

## Distribution and dependencies of the shape parameters

We first consider the marginal distributions of the PCA scores and wavelet coefficients, analysing their QQ-plots.

```{r param-qq, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "Normal Q-Q plots of the shape parameters: PCA scores PC1--PC6 (blue, top row) and wavelet parameters (orange), smooth coefficients S1--S8 followed by detail coefficients D1--D5. Points close to the black line indicate an approximately Normal parameter."}
plot_all_qq()
```

From Figure \@ref(fig:param-qq), we observe that PC1–PC4 lie approximately on the black line, with only minor deviations in the tails, although the largest values of PC2 fall below the line, indicating a lighter upper tail. PC5 shows heavy tails on either side, while PC6 deviates substantially, with a particularly heavy lower tail. For wavelets, the 8 smooth coefficients lie approximately on the black line, other than at the extreme ends, where S1–S3 and S8 show right skew, and S4 and S5, and to a lesser extent S6, level off at the extremes. Of the detail coefficients, D3 and D5 lie approximately on the line and D4 shows mild right skew, while D1 and D2 deviate heavily at the right tail.

As the majority of parameters sit approximately on the line through the centre of their distributions, we continue with our exploration of the Normal distribution, but due to some having heavy tails or large deviations at the extremes, we also consider a smoothed bootstrap sampling scheme, which does not require such a normality assumption.

We aim to fit each on shape parameters and the three standardisation parameters (peak flow, duration and peak position), which are held seperately. To justify this, we must consider their dependencies, and we use the Spearman correlations to do so.

```{r dependence-tables, echo = FALSE}
dependence_cols <- c("Peak flow", "Duration", "Peak position")

kables(
  list(
    kable(pca_dependence, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, valign = "t",
          col.names = dependence_cols),
    kable(wav_dependence, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, valign = "t",
          col.names = dependence_cols)
  ),
  format  = "latex",
  caption = "Spearman correlation of the shape parameters with the peak flow, duration and peak position of each event: PCA scores (left) and wavelet parameters (right).",
  label   = "dependence"
)
```

Table \@ref(tab:dependence) indicates moderate to strong correlations for both the PCA scores and the wavelet parameters with the standardisation parameters. In particular, PC2 and peak position have a correlation of $-0.80$, and S5 and peak position a correlation of $-0.74$, suggesting that standardisation does not fully separate the shape of a hydrograph from its timing. Simply fitting the unconditional distributions would therefore pair simulated shapes with peak flows, durations and peak positions that do not occur together in the data, as well as overstating the variation in shape for an event of a given size and timing. This motivates the need to move towards a conditional multivariate Normal distribution and a conditional smoothed bootstrap, which we fit in Section 5.2.

## Statistical model and sampling scheme

To fit the conditional multivariate Normal distribution and conditional smoothed bootstrap, we start in the same way.

Let $\boldsymbol{\theta}_i = (\theta_{i1}, \dots, \theta_{iK})^\top$ be the shape parameters for extreme flow event $i$, which are either the PCA scores ($K = 6$) or the wavelet coefficients ($K = 13$), and let $\mathbf{s}_i = (Q_i^{\text{peak}}, W_i, \tau_i)^\top$ be its standardisation parameters. We regress the shape parameters on the standardisation parameters,

$$
\boldsymbol{\theta}_i = \boldsymbol{\beta}_0 + B\,\mathbf{s}_i + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i,
$$

where $B$ is a $K \times 3$ matrix of coefficients, and fitting this by least squares gives residuals $\hat{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}_1, \dots, \hat{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}_N$ with sample covariance $\hat{\Sigma}$.

A new event with standardisation parameters $\mathbf{s}^\ast$ then has simulated shape parameters

$$
\boldsymbol{\theta}^\ast = \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_0 + \hat{B}\,\mathbf{s}^\ast + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\ast,
$$

where both approaches assume the residual spread is the same for every $\mathbf{s}^\ast$, and differ only in the generation of $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\ast$.

Our statistical model, the conditional Normal, generates $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\ast$ by assuming Normality for these residuals,

$$
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\ast \sim N_K(\mathbf{0}, \hat{\Sigma}).
$$

Our sampling scheme, the conditional smoothed bootstrap, generates $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\ast$ as

$$
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\ast = \frac{\hat{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}_J + h\,\mathbf{z}}{\sqrt{1+h^2}}, \qquad J \sim \text{Uniform}\{1,\dots,N\}, \quad \mathbf{z} \sim N_K(\mathbf{0}, \hat{\Sigma}),
$$

with $h = \big(4/((K+2)N)\big)^{1/(K+4)}$ (Silverman, 1986). The noise stops simulated residuals being exact copies of observed ones, and dividing by $\sqrt{1+h^2}$ keeps their covariance approximately at $\hat{\Sigma}$. Unlike the Normal, this keeps the heavy tails seen in Section \@ref(uncertainty).

Following the generation, we turn $\boldsymbol{\theta}^\ast$ into a curve using Equation \@ref(eq:pca) for PCA and \@ref(eq:wavelet) for wavelets, and finally we reverse the standardisation with $\mathbf{s}^\ast$.

## Evaluation criteria

We evaluate how well each approach simulates new extreme flow events using the criteria of coverage, continuous ranked probability score, and physical validity. For each, we simulate $M =$ `r n_each` shapes for event $i$ using its own standardisation parameters $\mathbf{s}_i$, then convert them to hydrographs $\hat{Q}_i^{(m)}(t_j)$, $m = 1, \dots, M$ and compare these with the observed hydrograph $Q_i(t_j)$ in $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ at the same `r n_grid` time points as in Section \@ref(evaluation-criteria). We average each criterion over all events.

**Coverage:** the percentage of the observed hydrograph lying inside the simulated 90\% band,

$$
\text{Coverage}_i = \frac{100}{118}\sum_{j} \mathbb{1}\big\{L_i(t_j) \le Q_i(t_j) \le U_i(t_j)\big\},
$$
where $L_i(t_j)$ and $U_i(t_j)$ are the 5\% and 95\% quantiles of the simulated flows at $t_j$. Coverage close to 90\% indicates that the simulated uncertainty is about right, while lower coverage indicates that the simulations are too narrow and higher coverage that they are too wide.

**Continuous ranked probability score (CRPS):** a measure of how close the simulated flows are to the observed flow, where simulations that are both accurate and appropriately spread perform better (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007),

$$
\text{CRPS}_i = \frac{1}{118}\sum_{j}\left( \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m} \big|\hat{Q}_i^{(m)}(t_j) - Q_i(t_j)\big| - \frac{1}{2M^2}\sum_{m}\sum_{m'} \big|\hat{Q}_i^{(m)}(t_j) - \hat{Q}_i^{(m')}(t_j)\big| \right).
$$
The first term is the average distance of the simulations from the observed flow, and the second subtracts half the average distance between simulations. For SEPA's approach, the second term is zero and the CRPS reduces to the mean absolute error, allowing a direct comparison. The result is in $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ and lower is better. 

**Physical validity:** the percentage of simulated standardised curves that are negative at any time point, and the percentage that rise more than 1\% above the peak value of one, both of which are not actually possible.

## Out-of-sample check

We now evaluate how our two approaches perform on events they have not seen, using a leave-one-out check repeated for each of the `r nrow(Y)` extreme flow events. For each event $i$, we remove it and refit both the shape method and the distribution to the other `r nrow(Y) - 1` events, then simulate 200 shapes using event $i$'s own peak flow, duration and peak position $\mathbf{s}_i$, before converting them to hydrographs and comparing them with event $i$'s observed hydrograph.

```{r out-of-sample, echo=FALSE}
kable(out_of_sample[, -1], format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("", "Coverage (\\%)", "CRPS (m$^3$/s)", "Negative flow (\\%)", "Above peak (\\%)"),
      escape = FALSE,
      caption = "Out-of-sample check: each event is left out of the fit, and 200 curves are simulated with its own peak flow, duration and peak position. Coverage: percentage of the observed curve inside the simulated 90\\% band (target 90\\%). CRPS: lower is better; for SEPA's single shape it is the mean absolute error. Last two columns: percentage of simulated curves that are physically invalid. Coverage, negative flow and above peak are measured on simulated curves, so do not apply to SEPA's single fixed shape.") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 9) %>%
  pack_rows("SEPA", 1, 1) %>%
  pack_rows("PCA", 2, 3) %>%
  pack_rows("Wavelets", 4, 5)
```

```{r held-out-bands, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=10, fig.cap="90\\% band of 200 simulated hydrographs for three contrasting extreme flow events, each left out of the fit, from each combination (rows), with the observed hydrograph in black."}
plot_held_out_bands()
```

From Table \@ref(tab:out-of-sample), all four combinations reduce the CRPS by at least `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (1 - max(out_of_sample$crps[-1]) / out_of_sample$crps[1]))`% compared with SEPA's fixed shape, for which the CRPS reduces to the mean absolute error, so simulating hydrographs from a fitted distribution is far more accurate than SEPA's current approach. Since the four differ in CRPS by no more than `r sprintf("%.2f", diff(range(out_of_sample$crps[-1])))` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$, we compare them on the remaining columns, which do not apply to SEPA as they are measured on simulated curves.

Coverage is below the 90% target for every combination, so the simulated bands are somewhat too narrow, partly because the variation discarded by keeping only $K$ components or coefficients cannot appear in them, and Figure \@ref(fig:held-out-bands) shows that the observed hydrographs leave the band mainly at secondary peaks. Wavelets have slightly higher coverage than PCA, by `r sprintf("%.1f", oos("Wavelets", "Conditional Normal", "coverage") - oos("PCA", "Conditional Normal", "coverage"))` percentage points for the Normal and `r sprintf("%.1f", oos("Wavelets", "Conditional bootstrap", "coverage") - oos("PCA", "Conditional bootstrap", "coverage"))` for the bootstrap, but more of their simulated curves are physically invalid, with around `r sprintf("%.0f", oos("Wavelets", "Conditional Normal", "above_peak"))`% rising above their peak compared with `r sprintf("%.0f", oos("PCA", "Conditional Normal", "above_peak"))`% for PCA, and more having negative flow. Finally, the Normal and bootstrap differ little on any measure, so the heavier tails kept by the bootstrap make no practical difference here.

## Simulating new extreme flow events {#uncertainty-sim}

In Subsection 6.4, we checked the models out of sample, now, we refit all four approaches to every event and use them to simulate new extreme flow events.

```{r fan-charts, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=8, fig.cap="Median, 25--75\\% and 5--95\\% bands of 1000 simulated standardised hydrographs from each combination, with the observed events in grey."}
plot_fan_charts()
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fan-charts) shows that all four approaches produce very similar overall shapes, as well as 50\% and 90\% bands. We see that the majority of observed events lie within the 90\% band, although in line with the analysis of the previous subsection, the main exceptions are multi-peaks on the recession. The bands also rise slightly above the peak just before it, and this is more pronounced for wavelets, where the bands also go below zero at the start of the event, demonstrating the higher percentage of negative flows from the previous subsection.

SEPA is primarily interested in how much land floods during an extreme flow event, which depends heavily on how much water passes through, so we move beyond our statistical evaluation criteria and consider the flood volume. Specifically, we take one typical event with the median peak flow, duration and peak position, so that these are held fixed and only the shape changes.

```{r volumes, echo=FALSE}
kable(volume_table, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("", "5\\%", "Median", "95\\%"), escape = FALSE,
      caption = paste0("Flood volume (million m$^3$) of an event with the median peak flow (",
                       round(typical["peak_flow"]), " m$^3$/s), duration and peak position: ",
                       "SEPA's single shape against 1000 simulated shapes from each scheme.")) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 9)
```

From Table \@ref(tab:volumes), applying SEPA's single fixed shape to this event gives a volume (the area under the hydrograph) of `r sprintf("%.1f", volume_table$median[1])` million $\text{m}^3$. On the other hand, simulating 1,000 plausible shapes for the same event from each of our four approaches gives median volumes of `r sprintf("%.1f", min(volume_table$median[-1]))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(volume_table$median[-1]))` million $\text{m}^3$, with a 90\% band of `r sprintf("%.1f", min(volume_table$lower, na.rm = TRUE))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(volume_table$upper, na.rm = TRUE))` million $\text{m}^3$.

This demonstrates that two events with the same peak flow can hold very different amounts of water just because of their shape, and SEPA's approach of fixing this shape and reporting just one number masks this entirely. Additionally, SEPA's volume sits above the 95th percentile of every approach, which suggests that SEPA's approach is not only missing this variation but may also systematically overestimate the volume, matching their large volume error in Section \@ref(cmp-accuracy). All four of our approaches produce very similar results, so this conclusion does not depend on which method or distribution is used.

## Other uncertainties

The uncertainty analysis we have conducted is based on our one observed set of `r nrow(Y)` extreme flow events, and we want to assess the extent to which our results depend on this particular set. To do so, for each of the four approaches, we create an alternative set of events by sampling our events at random with replacement, refit both the shape method and the distribution on this alternative set, and simulate 1,000 shapes, recording the edges of the 90\% band, repeating this 100 times.

```{r sampling, echo=FALSE}
kable(sampling_table, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("", "Band width", "SD of lower edge", "SD of upper edge"),
      caption = paste0("Sampling uncertainty: average width of the simulated 90\\% band, and the ",
                       "average standard deviation of its edges across ", n_boot,
                       " refits to resampled events (fractions of the peak flow)."),
      escape = FALSE) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 9)
```

From Table \@ref(tab:sampling), the band has an average width of around `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(sampling_table$band_width))` of the peak flow for every approach, while its edges move by only `r sprintf("%.3f", min(sampling_table[, c("lower_sd", "upper_sd")]))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", max(sampling_table[, c("lower_sd", "upper_sd")]))` between refits, around `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(unlist(sampling_table[, c("lower_sd", "upper_sd")])) / mean(sampling_table$band_width))`\% of its width. This suggests that our simulated uncertainty is relatively robust to the particular events observed, so our conclusions are unlikely to change substantially with a different set of similar events.

Comparing between approaches, we expected the wavelet bands to vary more between refits, since wavelets estimate many more quantities from the same events (`r ncol(wav_params)` shape parameters against `r k_chosen` for PCA). However, the standard deviations are almost identical across all four approaches, so sampling uncertainty does not distinguish between them, and provides no additional argument for parsimony.

Figure \@ref(fig:sampling-bands) shows that the most variation is in the lower (5\%) edge on the rising limb, where shapes differ most between events, while the upper (95\%) edge rises above the peak in every refit, demonstrating that this is a feature of the models rather than of the particular events observed.

```{r sampling-bands, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=8, fig.cap="Edges of the simulated 90\\% band from 100 refits to resampled events, for each combination."}
plot_sampling_bands()
```

# Recommendation and emulator application

## Recommendation

## Emulator application

Our recommended method, PCA, describes each extreme flow event by nine numbers: its peak flow, duration and peak position, and six principal component scores. These nine numbers become the emulator's inputs, which are now suitably low-dimensional, and SEPA would use the method in two stages.

**Collecting the data to fit the emulator:** SEPA must first choose the training inputs by selecting a few hundred combinations of the nine inputs using an experimental statistical design, such as a grid over the plausbile parameter ranges [@wilson2026lec3]. Each combination would then be turned into a hydrograph as before, reconstruvting the standardised shape from the six scores using Equation (), and then reversing the standardisation using the peak flow, duration and peak position. Each hydrograph is then ran through the flood inundation model and the outputs of interest, such as maximum flood depth or the total flooded area, are recorded. An emulator is then fitted to these pairs of inputs and outputs and checked against a set of runs held back from fitting, so that it can approximate the flood inundation model at a fraction of the computational cost.

**Using the emulator to explore uncertainty in flood inundation:** Following this, SEPA can then use our conditional multivariate Normal distribution from Section \@ref(uncertainty) to simulate a large number of new extreme flow events. Since the emulator can be evaluated much more quickly than the inundation model, thousands of these events can be passed through to give a full distribution of flood depths or extents that reflects parametric uncertainty, meaning uncertainty in both the size and shape of the hydrograph. The emulator's own prediction uncertainty at untested inputs, known as function uncertainty [@wilson2026lec3], show also be added to this distribution, as well as any structural discrepancy that remains between the inundation model and real flooding, and between our statistical model and the real variation in hydrograph shape. Our Normality assumption and the simulated bands containing around 81\% of observed events both contribute to this.

Finally, repeating this with the scores fixed at zero which corresponds to the average shape, would also show how much of the uncertainty in flood inundation is due to hydrograph shape alone, which SEPA's current approach does not capture.
